personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Snape is defined by a dense cluster of observable traits: cold menace delivered in controlled, measured language ('in his most dangerous voice,' 'said Snape silkily,' 'said Snape coldly'); calculated cruelty toward specific targets, especially Neville, Harry, and Lupin; petty vindictiveness expressed through institutional power (point-docking, detentions, weaponizing homework); barely restrained contempt for James Potter projected onto Harry ('How extraordinarily like your father you are'); suppressed triumph that surfaces when he believes he has an advantage; and periodic explosions of uncontrolled rage when humiliated or thwarted (the Shrieking Shack sequence: 'KEEP QUIET, YOU STUPID GIRL!', 'YOU DON'T KNOW POTTER!'). His voice is characteristically low, slow, and deliberate — the silkiness and the softness are weapons. His cruelty toward Neville is systemic and public. His loathing of Lupin is rooted in an old wound. He is not simply cruel; he is shrewd and calculating, with moments where emotional control breaks catastrophically. He also has a watchful, suspicious intelligence (examining the one-eyed witch, using the Floo to summon Lupin, tracking Harry on the map).
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves Snape's core register: cold, contemptuous, deliberate. 'Turn to page 394' is iconic precisely because it delivers menace through bureaucratic terseness. His treatment of Hermione ('Are you incapable of restraining yourself? Or do you take pride in being an insufferable know-it-all?') matches the book's pattern of weaponized classroom authority. His confrontation with Harry in the corridor ('How extraordinarily like your father you are, Potter. He, too, was exceedingly arrogant') faithfully reproduces the book's language almost verbatim. His behavior in the Shrieking Shack — smug arrival, wand at Lupin's chest, the 'Ah, vengeance is sweet' line, the fanatical gleam — is consistent with the book's portrayal of a man who has lost rational perspective in the grip of an old grudge. His film voice retains the trademark quiet menace and sardonic edge ('Should you die, I assure you... you need not hand it in').
personality_voice.difference: Two meaningful losses. First, Snape's systematic, scene-by-scene classroom bullying of Neville is almost entirely absent from the film corpus. The book establishes this as a dominant recurring pattern: Snape humiliates Neville publicly, forces him to perform under threat, makes him the object of class-wide spectacle, and then exploits his work product (the shrinking solution) to dock points from Gryffindor anyway. This is not a single scene — it is a portrait of sustained institutional cruelty that defines a core personality trait. The film's boggart scene shows the Boggart-Snape briefly, but the actual Snape does not bully Neville in the classroom in the film corpus. Second, and more significantly, the film omits the post-Shrieking Shack eruption — Snape howling in the hospital wing, out of control, face twisted, spitting, beyond reason — which is the most explicit portrait of his emotional incontinence when humiliated. In the book this reads as a psychological portrait: the mask has cracked completely. The film's Shrieking Shack scene gives him some of this (the 'creature and the criminal' taunting, the 'Do I detect a flicker of fear?' sadism), but the post-revelation meltdown in the hospital wing is absent. His petty vindictiveness after the boggart incident (bullying Neville 'worse than ever,' the vindictive pleasure at Harry's failed potion) is also not present in the film corpus.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality — cold, controlled menace, personal loathing, suppressed triumph, sudden breaks into rage — is preserved in the film's key scenes. The losses are primarily the sustained texture of everyday classroom cruelty toward Neville and the complete psychological unraveling in the hospital wing. These are secondary traits in terms of screen time but primary traits in terms of characterization depth. The film preserves the dominant pattern but softens the texture. Score: 19 (main personality preserved, minor simplification and loss of secondary traits).

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Snape serves multiple narrative functions in PoA: (1) institutional antagonist and source of low-level dread throughout the year; (2) active investigator who suspects Lupin and acts on that suspicion (bringing the potion, watching Lupin, using the map); (3) the primary obstacle in the Shrieking Shack climax — it is his arrival that creates the dramatic crisis and he is the agent who binds Lupin, threatens Black, and forces the standoff; (4) the character whose version of events prevails at the end, determining that Sirius goes to the Kiss and Lupin loses his job; (5) the one who deliberately reveals Lupin's condition as an act of revenge. He is not decorative — he is a structural engine in at least three major plot sequences.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves his role as investigator (tracking Harry on the map, confronting him in the corridor, searching the castle). His Shrieking Shack arrival and confrontation are intact: he disarms Lupin and Black, threatens them, creates the standoff. The post-escape sequence shows his role in the hospital wing and corridor. His revealing of Lupin's condition is confirmed in the film (Lupin tells Harry: 'It seems that someone has let slip the nature of my condition' / Harry: 'Snape'). His report to Fudge and pursuit of institutional revenge are maintained.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Two agency losses. First, the film omits the Snape's Grudge chapter sequence where Snape catches Harry near the one-eyed witch, interrogates him in his office, discovers the Marauders' Map, and summons Lupin via Floo. In the book, this is an entire scene of active agency — Snape investigates, suspects, presses, and creates an important plot node. In the film this is compressed into a single corridor encounter at night where Lupin conveniently appears and intervenes, and the map interaction is much briefer and less dramatically rich. Snape's active investigative intelligence — the examination of the witch statue, the dungeon search, the systematic suspicion of Lupin — is present in fragments but not as fully realized. Second, and more critically, in the book Snape's version of events is what Dumbledore invokes when talking Harry and Hermione into the time-turn ('You must see that Professor Snape's version of events is far more convincing than yours'). In the film this is not present in the corpus, and the mechanism of Snape's narrative dominance after the fact is less developed. His role as the agent of Lupin's dismissal is confirmed but shown only in aftermath, not in the act of revelation.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Snape's role as primary antagonist-investigator and the Shrieking Shack pivot are preserved. The losses are in the richness of his investigative agency (the office sequence) and the full mechanics of his post-event revenge. He remains narratively functional but the film compresses two of his most active scenes into reduced forms. Score: 14 (role and agency are reduced but recognizable).

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Snape's motivations in PoA are layered and explicit: (1) professional rivalry and resentment toward Lupin rooted in a near-fatal humiliation at age sixteen — 'Sirius thought it would be amusing to tell Snape all he had to do was prod the knot'; (2) a personal loathing of James Potter, extended to Harry, rooted in the same episode and years of school rivalry; (3) a desire for institutional validation and recognition (wanting the DADA job, wanting the Order of Merlin, wanting credit for 'saving' Harry); (4) a genuine, if warped, sense of loyalty to Dumbledore and the system, which he operates within rather than against; (5) the old wound of humiliation that overrides reason in the Shrieking Shack — 'You fool,' said Lupin. 'Is a schoolboy grudge worth putting an innocent man back inside Azkaban?' Snape's internal conflict is between his genuine intelligence and professional competence on one hand, and the festering grievance that makes him irrational when Lupin, Black, or James-by-proxy-Harry is involved.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core motivations. His confrontation with Harry explicitly references James: 'How extraordinarily like your father you are, Potter. He, too, was exceedingly arrogant.' The Shrieking Shack shows his triumphalism and obsessive focus on Black as personal revenge: 'Ah, vengeance is sweet. How I hoped I'd be the one to catch you.' Lupin's backstory — the Whomping Willow prank, Snape's near-death, his lifelong resentment — is present in dialogue (Lupin explains to the children: 'Professor Snape was at school with us'... though this is absent from the film corpus, the film does establish the core dynamic). His desire for credit and institutional reward is shown in the hospital wing corridor (Fudge promising him an Order of Merlin). His motivation for revealing Lupin's condition is confirmed as revenge.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film does not contain the explicit Lupin monologue (book scenes 292–296) explaining the full backstory of the Whomping Willow incident, Snape's near-death, James saving him, and the decades of resentment. This is present in the book Shrieking Shack sequence and gives Snape's motivations full psychological depth — including the uncomfortable detail that James saved his life and Snape regards it as no act of heroism. In the film corpus, this backstory is implied rather than stated. Snape's confrontation with Harry about James in the corridor scene exists ('How extraordinarily like your father you are') but the full 'your father saved my life but I owe him nothing' speech from the books (scenes 213–225) is absent from the film corpus — the corridor scene is shorter and cuts before that passage. The motivation is correct but the psychological complexity behind it is underexplained.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are present and essentially correct — personal grudge, resentment, desire for revenge and recognition. The loss is in the full psychological elaboration of why those grudges run so deep and why they make him irrational. The film preserves the 'what' but partially loses the 'why.' Score: 11 (motivations simplified but still correct).
motivations_internal_conflict.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for the film; reasonably inferred for the depth of the backstory loss

character_arc.book_baseline: Within PoA specifically, Snape does not undergo a traditional arc of change. His starting point and ending point are the same: he is resentful, suspicious of Lupin, obsessed with his grievance, and professionally thwarted. What he has is a dramatic arc of revelation and defeat: he suspects Lupin from the start, acts on his suspicion, briefly achieves his goal (capturing Black and Lupin), is humiliated again (knocked out, overridden by events, Black escapes), and then retaliates by revealing Lupin's condition — a final act of pettiness that confirms rather than resolves his character. This is an intentionally flat moral arc: Snape does not learn or grow; he doubles down. The 'arc' is one of thematic demonstration — his schoolboy grudge does exactly what Lupin accuses it of: it nearly gets an innocent man killed and it punishes a good teacher. His last act in the book is motivated purely by spite.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film follows this same non-arc faithfully. He suspects, investigates, achieves temporary triumph in the Shrieking Shack, is overridden and humiliated, and retaliates by exposing Lupin. The flat moral arc — grudge unresolved, pettiness confirmed — is present. Lupin's resignation is confirmed as Snape's doing.
character_arc.difference: The film's primary compression is the loss of the extended falling action: the hospital wing meltdown, the full conversation between Snape and Fudge about Harry's punishment, and the extended aftermath of Snape's behavior being remarked upon ('Fellow seems quite unbalanced,' says Fudge; the exam results note that Dumbledore may have saved Harry from being failed by Snape deliberately). These moments in the book don't change the arc but they complete it — they show the full consequence of Snape's behavior and the degree to which even his supposed allies find him excessive. The film captures the arc's shape but not its full resolution.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc is compressed but faithful. The intentional flatness is preserved — Snape is the same person at the end as at the beginning, and his final act of revenge confirms it. Score: 13 (arc compressed but still faithful).

key_relationships.book_baseline: Snape's key relationships in PoA are: (1) Snape–Lupin: old enemies, sustained antagonism rooted in near-death experience, professional resentment, and mutual history; Snape suspects, undermines, and ultimately destroys Lupin's position; (2) Snape–Harry: personal loathing projected from James, a power dynamic of institutional authority used as a weapon, with Harry as a proxy target for older hatred; (3) Snape–Dumbledore: subordinate who chafes against Dumbledore's tolerance of Lupin, who is shut down when he presses, who watches Dumbledore with 'an expression of deep resentment' — a relationship of constrained loyalty and simmering disagreement; (4) Snape–Neville: predatory classroom dynamic where Snape uses institutional authority to terrorize a vulnerable student, with no narrative justification beyond evident cruelty and possibly the enjoyment of power.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: Snape–Lupin is well preserved: the antagonism is explicit, the old grudge motivates his behavior throughout, the confrontation in the Shrieking Shack captures the depth of the hatred. Snape–Harry is preserved in the key dialogue scenes (corridor, classroom). Snape–Dumbledore: the film has the exchange after the Fat Lady attack — Snape tries to implicate Lupin, Dumbledore shuts him down with a warning tone, and Snape watches Dumbledore with resentment. This is present and faithful. Snape–Neville: almost entirely absent from the film corpus. The boggart scene shows Neville's fear of Snape, but the actual dynamic — Snape deliberately terrorizing Neville in class, the shrinking solution sequence, the toad-as-test-subject threat — is not present in the film corpus.
key_relationships.difference: The Snape–Neville relationship is the significant loss. In the books, this is a recurring and defining dynamic: it reveals Snape's willingness to use institutional power to destroy a vulnerable child's confidence, it establishes the depth of his cruelty beyond mere professional rivalry, and it is what makes him Neville's boggart. The film gestures at this (Neville naming Snape as his greatest fear) but does not show the relationship that produces that fear. The other three key relationships are adequately preserved.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Three of four key relationships are preserved with appropriate dynamics. The Snape–Neville dynamic is gestured at but not demonstrated. The result is that the film's Snape is understood to be feared by Neville without showing us why, which weakens both the relationship and the character's portrait as a systematic abuser of power. Score: 7 (relationships mostly faithful, one important dynamic significantly weakened).

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: What makes PoA's Snape rich beyond his surface villainy: (1) the classroom scenes are not just cruelty — they show a meticulous, performative sadism (the toad test, the point-docking after Neville succeeds, the timing of humiliations for maximum effect) that reveals a specific psychological profile; (2) the contradiction between his intelligence and his irrationality — he is the most competent Potions master at Hogwarts, brews a complex and rare potion for Lupin faithfully, and yet is undone by a schoolboy grudge; (3) the ambiguity of his motivations: is he bringing Lupin's potion out of genuine duty, or is he watching for evidence? The book suggests both; (4) the full Shrieking Shack breakdown — 'beyond reason,' 'seemed beyond reason,' 'mad glint in Snape's eyes' — is the most explicit portrait of his psychological instability; (5) the aftermath where his behavior alarms even Fudge and where Dumbledore may have had to protect Harry from his deliberate sabotage; (6) the detail that he reveals Lupin's condition 'accidentally' at breakfast — a cowardly, petty act that he cannot even own directly; (7) the observation that his 'dislike of Harry could increase' after the Shrieking Shack episode, with physical symptoms of barely restrained violence.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves: the Shrieking Shack sadism and fanaticism, the classroom contempt, the corridor confrontation with Harry, the institutional maneuvering. It loses: the full classroom texture with Neville, the complete psychological unraveling in the hospital wing, the extended post-event aftermath showing the consequences and limits of his behavior, and the full Marauder's Map sequence in his office which is one of the richest portraits of his investigative intelligence and his petty institutional power.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film's Snape is recognizably complex — he is not reduced to a single note. But the specific texture that makes him so rich in the book is significantly thinned. The systematic Neville cruelty, the ambiguity of the potion delivery, the full hospital wing meltdown, the 'accidentally let slip' cowardice of the Lupin reveal, and the post-book aftermath are all absent or compressed. What remains is a Snape who is menacing, grudge-driven, and fanatical in key moments — but who lacks the sustained, granular portrait of petty institutional evil and psychological complexity the books provide.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film preserves the headline traits and several key nuanced moments (the Shrieking Shack fanaticism, the sardonic classroom voice, the suppressed triumph). What is lost is the sustained texture, the Neville dynamic, the ambiguity of the potion scenes, and the full psychological portrait. This is noticeable simplification — the character remains substantially recognizable but several important nuances are missing. Score: 9.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.evidence_status: Directly evidenced for what is present; reasonably inferred for what is absent based on corpus comparison

key_observations: The film's Snape is broadly faithful in his dominant traits — cold menace, grudge-driven irrationality, sardonic classroom authority, fanatical behavior in the Shrieking Shack — and the core of his voice and personality is well preserved. However, the film loses two things that are genuinely defining in the books: the sustained, granular portrait of his classroom cruelty toward Neville (which is the most consistent evidence of his character across the year, not just a single scene), and the full psychological collapse in the hospital wing (the most explicit portrait of his instability when humiliated). The compression of the Marauder's Map office sequence also removes his most active scene of investigative agency. What remains is a Snape who hits the high dramatic notes but lacks the sustained everyday texture and the full portrait of psychological fragility beneath the controlled menace. The score of 73 reflects a character who is recognizably and substantially faithful in his key moments, but who has been meaningfully simplified in the material that made him most complex.
